**Keywords:** PARAFAC2, tensor decomposition, cell--cell communication, scRNA-seq, ligand--receptor interactions, multi-condition

**Abstract:**

Cell--cell communication (CCC) coordinates cellular activities that vary dynamically across time, location, and biological context.
Most computational tools infer CCC by aggregating cells into predefined types, obscuring the single-cell heterogeneity that distinguishes functional subpopulations; conversely, the methods that do preserve single-cell resolution cannot model how communication is regulated across multiple conditions.
To bridge this gap, we developed CCC-RISE, an extension of the tensor-based method Reduction and Insight in Single-cell Exploration (RISE).
Rather than relying on cell-type labels, CCC-RISE uses PARAFAC2-derived eigen-states to deconvolve communication into interpretable programs defined by sender cells, receiver cells, ligand--receptor pairs, and conditions, then maps each program back to the individual cells that drive it.
Applied to a lung transplant cohort with acute allograft dysfunction, CCC-RISE identified sender and receiver subpopulations with more granularity than available cell-type annotations and recovered coordinated communication programs that associated with disease outcome.
For example, fibrotic BTC--EGFR signaling was a common feature among lung transplant patients that CCC-RISE subdivided into ciliated epithelial sender cells and basal/secretory epithelial receiver cells.
CCC-RISE thus resolves disease-relevant signaling subpopulations that are invisible to aggregate methods by analyzing multi-condition data while preserving single-cell resolution.

**Highlights:**

- CCC-RISE analyzes cell--cell communication across conditions at single-cell resolution, without relying on predefined cell-type labels

- It deconvolves communication into interpretable programs defined by sender cells, receiver cells, ligand--receptor pairs, and conditions

- Mapping programs back to individual cells reveals mutually exclusive signaling subpopulations whose granularity exceeds that of available annotations

- In a lung transplant cohort, CCC-RISE identifies a coordinated communication axis associated with allograft function and patient survival
